references.text: The parallel account in the Gospel of Mark about the poor widow who put two small coins into the temple treasury [ref:Mark 12:42-44|Markus 12:42-44] provides the most detailed parallel, where Jesus also sees the widow putting in her two small coins and comments that she gave more than all the others.

God's care for widows is a recurring theme in the OT. [ref:5 Mos 24:17|5. Mosebok 24:17] forbids perverting justice for the widow, showing God's special attention toward this vulnerable group—the same group Jesus notices here.

The widow in Zarephath in [ref:1 Kong 17:10-16|1. Kongebok 17:10-16] gave from her poverty what little she had to the prophet Elijah. She is an Old Testament example of the poor widow who gives all she has, trusting in God.

Paul describes the churches in Macedonia as giving generously out of their deep poverty [ref:2 Kor 8:2-3|2. Korinterbrev 8:2-3]. The principle is the same as with the poor widow: generosity that springs from poverty and devotion, not from abundance.
The preceding verse [ref:Luk 21:1|Lukas 21:1] sets the scene by describing Jesus watching the rich put their gifts into the temple treasury, which forms a contrast to the poor widow in verse 2.

In [ref:Luk 21:3-4|Lukas 21:3-4], Jesus gives his assessment of the widow's gift: she gave more than all the others, for they gave out of their abundance, but she gave out of her poverty all she had to live on. This expands on the meaning of what is described in verse 2.
[ref:Sal 68:6|Salmene 68:6] describes God as "the widow's provider", showing that the God who sees the poor widow in the temple is the same one who has always cared for widows.

The widow in the parable in [ref:Luk 18:3-5|Lukas 18:3-5] is another example in Luke's Gospel where a poor widow is presented as an example—here, of perseverance in prayer. Luke shows special attention toward widows and the poor.
